newsitem.title: USA: Cream found to reduce pain in infant circumcision.
newsitem.headline: Cream found to reduce pain in infant circumcision.

text.p: A cream containing two painkillers can ease a newborn's pain as he is being circumcised, according to a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine.
An editorial accompanying the article suggests parents insist that the cream be used.

Traditionally, most doctors have not given painkillers to a newborn before cutting the foreskin of the penis because they regarded circumcision as a minor procedure and were concerned about potential side-effects of the drugs on the infant.

But some studies have suggested that the pain caused by the circumcision can alter sleeping, feeding, and crying patterns, and even affect how much pain a child feels during a routine vaccination four months later.
A pain-numbing cream could help solve the problem.

The cream used in the study, sold under the brand name Emla in both the United States and Canada by Astra Ab, contained a combination of lidocaine and prilocaine. It was applied directly to the area that was going to be cut.

Tests of 59 babies, half of whom got the medicine while the rest got a placebo cream with coconut oil, found that the babies who got the pain-numbing cream cried half as much, and that the typical heart rate was 10 beats less per minute, an indication that the babies were under less stress.
The newborns tended to cry during the procedure even if they received the anesthetic because the cream did not eliminate all pain.

"We recommend that (the cream's) use be considered routinely," said the team, led by Anna Taddio of the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto. Other techniques, such as giving the child a pacifier or sugar water, should also be used, they said.

In an editorial accompanying the article, Dr. Thomas Wiswell of Thomas Jefferson University in Philadelphia, praised the new study and said, "the current method of performing the procedure is still too barbaric.

"A more humane approach would be to swaddle the infant loosely, provide a pacifier" and use a less drastic restraining system, he said. A painkiller "should be provided in all cases. Parents and physicians should demand no less."

Circumcision itself has been a controversial procedure in recent years as people have questioned the value of the operation. The Journal estimated that at least 1.2 million to 1.8 million newborns are circumcised annually in the United States.
But a series of recent studies have revealed that there are important benefits to being circumcised.

Urinary tract infections, for example, are 12 times more common in uncircumcised infants. Circumcised men are at least 100 times less likely to develop cancer of the penis. The rate of sexually transmitted diseases, including HIV, is higher in uncircumcised men. Women are more likely to develop cervical cancer if their sexual partner is uncircumcised.
"Circumcision carries a low risk and provides protective benefits," said Wiswell.
